name: isAvailable is actually invoked somewhere vs method never called at all
side_a: No deduct: the response contains at least one actual invocation of isAvailable (with a String argument) on Account/this/implicitly, used to test the candidate username — the call exists in the code regardless of whether the surrounding loop logic is correct.
side_b: Deduct: the response never invokes isAvailable anywhere; it simply assigns the requested name (or otherwise sets username) without any availability check, so there is no call to award the point for.

name: Performs an availability check / search for a free name vs. unconditionally assigning the requested name
side_a: No deduct if the constructor actually consults isAvailable (directly or in a loop) and only sets username based on that check, i.e. it makes an attempt to find a usable/available name.
side_b: Deduct if the constructor never calls isAvailable and simply stores the requested name as the username, making no attempt to test or search for availability.

name: Counter must be advanced (++/+1) somewhere inside the loop body vs a declared-but-never-updated counter still counts
side_a: Deduct unless the counter's value actually changes once per repetition — i.e. a statement such as `i++`, `suffix++`, or `count = count + 1` executes inside the loop body. A counter that is only declared and then read (never updated) does not 'increment the count in the context of a loop' and loses the point.
side_b: Give the point (no_deduct) as long as a counter variable exists and is used inside the loop to build/test the candidate name, even if its value is never updated, treating the declaration plus in-loop use as sufficient evidence of counting.

name: Tries the unmodified requestedName before appending digits vs. never tests the bare name
side_a: no_deduct — the answer explicitly tests the unsuffixed requestedName for availability and assigns it when available (e.g. `if (isAvailable(requestedName)) { username = requestedName; }`) before falling back to numbered variants.
side_b: deduct — the answer never evaluates the bare requestedName as a candidate: it either assigns it blindly with no availability test, or jumps straight into appending numbers so the plain name can never be chosen.

name: Numeric suffix sequence begins at 1 vs. begins at 0
side_a: no_deduct — the appended counter is initialized to 1, so the first fallback candidate is requestedName+"1" as the problem requires.
side_b: deduct — the appended counter starts at 0 (or any value other than 1), producing requestedName+"0" as the first fallback candidate.
